turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Hi, come on in. Have a seat anywhere. I'm Priya Natarajan, one of the psychiatric nurse practitioners here. Can you tell me your full name and date of birth?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Daniella Restripo, May 8,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: 1992. Thank you, Daniella. Did you find parking okay? That garage is a bit of a maze.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yes, I ended up all the way on the roof, but it's fine.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: That happens to everyone, so your primary care doctor sent you over. Tell me, in your own words, what's been going on.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Um, I've just been really down. For about three months now, I don't enjoy anything anymore. I used to paint on the weekends, and I haven't touched it since June.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I'm sorry. That sounds really hard. How's your sleep been?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Bad, I fall asleep okay, but I wake up around 4 in the morning and I can't get back to sleep.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: And you're appetite.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm just not hungry. I think I've lost maybe 8 pounds without trying.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: What about energy and concentration?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Low energy all the time. At work I read the same email like 3 times. I'm a project coordinator at Halverson Engineering, and I'm, you know,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: kind of barely keeping up. Did anything happen that set this off?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My relationship ended in the spring, five years, but honestly it feels bigger than that now.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: That makes sense. Have you ever had a stretch like this before? Or been treated for depression or anxiety?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, this is the first time I've never been on anything for it.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Have you ever had times where you felt the opposite, like really high energy, barely needing sleep for days, racing thoughts.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, never,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: anyone in your family,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: with depression,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: or bipolar disorder.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: My aunt on my dad's side has bipolar, I think, and my sister Paola takes something for anxiety, I don't know what.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Okay, that's helpful.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Now,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I'm going to ask a couple of questions, I ask everyone, have you had any thoughts that you'd be better off dead, or thoughts of hurting yourself.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No, I feel awful but know nothing like that.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Any thoughts of hurting anyone else?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: No!

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Thank you for answering that. How about alcohol or drugs?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Maybe a glass of wine once a week. No drugs. Any medical problems.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: And are you allergic to any medications?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: I'm healthy otherwise. I'm allergic to penicillin. I break out in hives. got it.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: So the questionnaire you filled out in the waiting room, the PHQ -9, your score is 15, which is in the moderate range. Your G, a D -7 anxiety score is 6.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: So mild,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: your blood pressure The pressure today is 116 over 74, pulse 72, and your weight is 138 pounds, and so you know what I'm noting. You're well -groomed, your speech is normal, your mood is sad, and your effect is a bit flat, and your thinking is clear and organized.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Yeah, that sounds about right.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: So here's what I think. this looks like major depression, a single episode,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: moderate.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: The good news is it's very treatable. What I'd like to do is start sertraline, 25 milligrams once a day for one week, then go up to 50 milligrams once a day. It can take four to six weeks to really feel the difference.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Are there side effects?

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Some people get an upset stomach or a headache the first week or two, and that usually fades. Take it with breakfast. And because of your aunt's history, if you ever notice you're suddenly wired, not sleeping but not tired, call us right away.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I'd also like you to start therapy, so I'm putting in a referral to our therapy team for weekly sessions, and I'm giving you this safety plan card. If you ever do have thoughts of hurting yourself, you can call or text 988, the crisis line,

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: anytime,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: or go to the nearest emergency room.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Okay, thank you.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Which pharmacy do you use?

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Lakeview Pharmacy on 4120 Belmont Avenue.

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: I'll send it there. And what's the best number number to reach you,

turns.speaker: clinician
turns.text: Great. Let's see you back in four weeks on October 19th to check how you're doing on the medicine.

turns.speaker: patient
turns.text: Sounds good. Thanks, really.
